title: Caffeine metabolism · CYP1A2
summary: CYP1A2 is a liver enzyme that clears most caffeine. A common DNA change, rs762551, affects how strongly this enzyme responds. The change is often written as CYP1A2 -163C>A. People with two A copies clear caffeine faster on average. People with a C copy clear it more slowly.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele, the genotype associated with faster caffeine clearance on average (sometimes called the 'fast metabolizer' genotype). In the Cornelis 2006 study, heavy coffee intake was not linked to higher heart-attack risk in this group. Actual caffeine sensitivity still varies a lot with smoking, medications, body size and habit.
interpretations.AC: One A and one C allele. The C allele is associated with lower CYP1A2 inducibility, so caffeine tends to be cleared somewhat more slowly than in AA individuals, on average. Many other factors (smoking strongly induces CYP1A2, some medications inhibit it) shift caffeine clearance more than this genotype does.
interpretations.CC: Two C copies are linked to slower caffeine clearance on average. Some studies found more sleep problems after caffeine. Cornelis 2006 also found a modest rise in heart attack risk with very high coffee intake. These are group averages, not a forecast for one person.

title: Muscle composition · ACTN3 R577X
summary: ACTN3 makes alpha-actinin-3, a protein in fast-twitch muscle fibers. The T copy of rs1815739, also called R577X, adds a stop signal. People with two T copies make none of this protein. This common, harmless type is seen more often in elite endurance athletes and less often in elite sprint or power athletes.

interpretations.CC: Two working ACTN3 copies are also called 577RR. Fast-twitch muscle fibers make alpha-actinin-3. Studies find this type more often in elite sprint and power athletes. For daily training, the effect is small. Training history and many other genes matter much more.
interpretations.CT: One working copy and one stop copy are also called 577RX. The body still makes alpha-actinin-3. Studies of elite athletes often place this type between the other two groups. They show no stable effect on daily performance.
interpretations.TT: Two stop copies are also called 577XX. The body makes no alpha-actinin-3. About one in five people with European ancestry share this harmless type. It is seen a little more often in elite endurance athletes and less often in elite sprinters. It says very little about one person's athletic ability.

citations.label: Yang et al., Am J Hum Genet 2003

title: Endurance trainability · PPARGC1A Gly482Ser
summary: PPARGC1A makes PGC-1α, which helps muscle cells build mitochondria. The Gly482Ser change is rs8192678. The T copy here marks Ser482. Some studies link Gly482 to endurance athletes and response to aerobic training. Other studies do not, so this is a weak signal.

interpretations.CC: Two Gly482 copies are shown as C on the forward strand. Reviews find this type a little more often in endurance athletes than in the public. Any effect on aerobic ability is small beside training. Several studies found no link at all.
interpretations.CT: One Gly482 and one Ser482 copy. Studies that report a difference generally place heterozygotes in between the homozygous groups; many studies find no measurable difference for carriers of one Ser482 allele.
interpretations.TT: Two Ser482 copies are shown as T on the forward strand and A in gene-strand papers. Some studies link this type to a slightly weaker response to aerobic training. It is also seen less often in elite endurance athletes. Results conflict, and any real effect is small.

title: Vitamin D levels · CYP2R1
summary: CYP2R1 makes the main liver enzyme that turns vitamin D into the form measured in blood, 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Studies repeatedly link rs10741657 near this gene to blood levels. The A copy is linked to slightly higher levels and G to slightly lower levels. Sun, food, latitude, season, and body weight matter much more.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies are linked to slightly higher 25-hydroxyvitamin D in blood on average. Wang 2010 found only a small effect for each copy, a few percent of a usual blood level. This type does not ensure that a vitamin D level is high enough.
interpretations.AG: One A and one G allele: intermediate on average. The difference between genotype groups is a small shift in average blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D; lifestyle and season shift levels far more than this variant does.
interpretations.GG: Two G copies are linked to slightly lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D in blood on average. Wang 2010 found a modest rise in the chance of falling below common target levels. The shift is small. Only a blood test can show the actual level.

title: Vitamin B12 levels · FUT2
summary: FUT2 helps decide whether certain sugars appear on cells in the gut. Some DNA changes reduce this secretor function. They are repeatedly linked to higher vitamin B12 in blood, perhaps through gut bacteria such as H. pylori. At rs602662, A marks reduced function and slightly higher B12. G marks secretor status and slightly lower B12.

interpretations.GG: Two G copies mark secretor function. Large studies link this type to somewhat lower vitamin B12 in blood on average. This is not a finding of deficiency. Food and health conditions that affect absorption matter much more.
interpretations.AG: One G and one A allele: average measured B12 in this group falls between the two homozygous groups in large cohort studies. The genotype effect is modest relative to diet and other absorption factors.
interpretations.AA: Two A copies mark reduced FUT2 secretor function. Studies link this type to higher vitamin B12 in blood on average. This group result does not rule out a B12 deficiency, especially when a diet contains little B12.

title: Omega-3/6 fatty acid conversion · FADS1
summary: FADS1 helps turn short plant fats, such as ALA from flax, into long-chain omega-3 and omega-6 fats, such as EPA and arachidonic acid. The nearby rs174537 change strongly tracks blood levels of these fats. G copies are linked to better conversion and T copies to lower conversion. People with T copies may gain more from ready-made EPA and DHA in fish.

interpretations.GG: Two G copies are linked to a more active FADS1 enzyme. For the same diet, this group has more long-chain fats in the blood. These include arachidonic acid and EPA. Tanaka 2009 found that this DNA region explained a large part of the difference in arachidonic acid.
interpretations.GT: One G and one T copy give conversion in the middle on average. With a similar diet, long-chain fat levels in blood tend to fall between the two other groups.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies are linked to weaker conversion of plant fats such as ALA into long-chain omega-3 and omega-6 fats. With the same intake, this group has lower arachidonic acid and EPA on average. Ready-made EPA and DHA from food add more to their long-chain omega-3 levels.

title: Iron status · TMPRSS6 V736A
summary: TMPRSS6 helps control hepcidin, a hormone that sets how much iron the gut takes in. The common rs855791 change, also called V736A, is repeatedly linked to iron measures. A, the valine form, tracks slightly lower iron and hemoglobin. G, the alanine form, tracks slightly higher levels. Most shifts are small and within the usual range.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies mark the 736Val form. Studies link this type to slightly lower iron, transferrin saturation, and hemoglobin on average. Each copy changes hemoglobin by less than one gram per liter. Food, periods, and blood donation matter much more. Only a blood test shows iron status.
interpretations.AG: One A and one G allele: iron measures in this group average between the two homozygous groups in large population studies. The genotype contributes only a small nudge relative to dietary and physiological factors.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele (736Ala), associated on average with slightly higher serum iron and hemoglobin. This is a modest population-level shift, not protection against iron deficiency or a sign of iron overload.

title: Sleep duration · ABCC9
summary: ABCC9 helps form a potassium channel that senses energy in cells. A 2013 review of European groups linked rs11046205 to usual sleep length and estimated that it explained about 5% of the difference. A fly study also changed sleep by reducing the matching gene. A much larger UK Biobank study found no link, so this result is not confirmed.

interpretations.GG: This is the most common type at the ABCC9 change. The 2013 study linked it to somewhat shorter sleep than types with an A copy. A later UK Biobank study of more than 127,000 people found almost no effect. This result cannot show how much sleep one person needs.
interpretations.AG: One A copy was linked to longer sleep reported by participants in the 2013 study. The much larger UK Biobank study did not find the same link. This result is unclear for sleep length.
interpretations.AA: Two A copies were linked to the longest sleep reported by participants in the 2013 study. A much larger later study did not find the same result. This is an early, unconfirmed link, not a sound guide to sleep needs.

title: Morning chronotype · RGS16
summary: Being a morning person is partly inherited. In a 23andMe study of 89,283 people, the strongest single signal was near RGS16, which helps control body-clock signals. At rs516134, the rare C copy was linked to a higher chance of calling yourself a morning person: a small shift. Hundreds of genes, age, light, and habits matter, so this change has little effect.

interpretations.CC: Two C copies are linked to morning preference. This type is rare; only a few percent of people with European ancestry carry C. The group has a modest rise in the chance of calling themselves a morning person. One DNA change explains very little because hundreds help shape sleep timing.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the C allele, associated with higher odds of self-reporting as a morning person in the Hu 2016 genome-wide study. This is a small shift on average in a highly polygenic trait, not a determinant of your actual sleep timing.
interpretations.TT: This is the most common type and has no C copy linked to morning preference. The result says little on its own. Hundreds of DNA changes, age, light, and daily habits shape sleep timing. Many people with TT strongly prefer mornings.

title: Vitamin C levels · SLC23A1
summary: SLC23A1 moves vitamin C from the gut and kidneys into blood. The uncommon rs33972313 change is linked to vitamin C in blood. In a study of about 15,000 people, each T copy tracked about 6 micromoles per liter less vitamin C. Usual levels are 40 to 60 micromoles per liter, so this shift is modest. Fruit and vegetables matter most.

interpretations.CC: The common type has no T copy that reduces transport. Vitamin C still depends mainly on food. This result suggests no unusual effect from this DNA change on how the body handles vitamin C.
interpretations.CT: One T copy was linked to about 6 micromoles per liter less vitamin C in blood on average in Timpson 2010. This is a modest group shift. Food changes levels much more, and this result does not show a measured level.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies form a rare type. Only a few percent of people with European ancestry carry T. This group had the lowest vitamin C in blood on average. The estimated effect is still small beside food. It describes a group average, not one person's level.

citations.label: Timpson et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2010
